# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles individually assessed population series for 56.360 urban centres, garrison foundations (*amsar*), fortified towns (*kastra*) and caravan hubs across 25 modern national jurisdictions from 632AD to 1000AD. Vetted from 56.610 evaluated candidates after excluding 250 unquantified minor scatters, subordinate suburbs, duplicate aliases and architectural fragments, the dataset tracks 6.301 active centres housing 15,7M inhabitants in 632AD, 23.633 active centres housing 17,16M in 750AD, 42.129 active centres housing 23,4M at the 850AD Abbasid zenith and 53.230 centres housing 27,83M in 1000AD ($\alpha = 1,22$, $R^2 = 0,94$). Grouped into six geographic divisions covering Iraq and al-Jazira, Bilad al-Sham and Cyprus, Egypt, Iran and Afghanistan, Byzantine Anatolia and Caucasia, and North Africa with the Arabian Peninsula, the tables show how Rashidun garrison foundations (Basra, Kufa, Fustat, Kairouan), Umayyad regional capitals (Shiraz, Wasit, Ramla) and Abbasid river metropolises (Baghdad, Samarra, Raqqa) reshaped older Late Antique urban networks without extinguishing classical Mediterranean or Iranian oasis cities [@Nol2023Arab; @Bessard2018Politics; @ALJabri2023Developmen; @Bosworth2007Historic].



# Background

Urbanism across the Early Islamic Caliphate and its Byzantine and Caucasian frontiers was neither a sterile preservation of Hellenistic civic geometry nor an abrupt collapse into nomadic pasture. Between 632AD and 1000AD, old Roman, Byzantine and Sassanid cities coexisted with planned Muslim foundations whose street grids, congregational mosques, *suq* market halls and waterworks answered fiscal and military imperatives [@Allahham2025Untold; @Yassin2012Architectu; @Bessard2018Politics]. In Iraq and Egypt, the Rashidun conquests immediately generated purpose-built garrison camps (*amsar*) at Basra (638AD), Kufa (638AD) and Fustat (641AD), followed in Ifriqiya by Kairouan (670AD) [@Nol2023Arab; @ALJabri2023Developmen; @Bosworth2007Historic]. Positioned along navigable river margins or desert-steppe interfaces where tribal cavalry could assemble without billeting inside existing civic quarters, these camps quickly grew into permanent craft and trading cities sustained by *kharaj* grain and silver stipends [@Yuksel2024Mecca; @Isoldi2026Confluent].

Under the Umayyad caliphs (661AD to 750AD), planned foundations multiplied across Syria, Palestine, Fars and lower Mesopotamia. Governors laid out Shiraz (693AD) and Wasit (702AD) as military-administrative capitals, while Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik established al-Ramla (c. 715AD) as the provincial capital of Jund Filastin, displacing coastal Caesarea without erasing inland market towns such as Tiberias, Amman and Damascus [@Nol2021Defining; @Stern2025Mamluk; @Ali2026Dimensions]. The Abbasid transfer of the seat of power to Iraq in 750AD shifted metropolitan gravity east again. Al-Mansur's Round City of Baghdad (762AD) and al-Mu'tasim's palace-garrison belt at Samarra (836AD) towered over the Tigris corridor, supported by the dense canal networks of the Sawad [@ALJabri2023Developmen; @Wahhab2024Decorative]. Further east, Tahirid, Samanid and Buyid patronage turned Rayy, Nishapur, Isfahan, Shiraz, Balkh and Herat into high-density *qanat*-fed manufacturing metropolises on the Silk Roads [@Saatsaz2023Technology; @Lu2023Connected; @Michailidis2014Dynastic]. Meanwhile, in Byzantine Anatolia, seventh-century raids compressed open *poleis* into fortified hilltop *kastra* such as Amorium, Ancyra, Ephesus and Caesarea before ninth- and tenth-century frontier stability renewed provincial towns [@Coleman2021Poleis; @Bakirtzis2023Introducin; @Navruz2024Historical].

# Methodology

The 56.360 individually assessed settlement entries tabulated here represent the vetted urban core of 56.610 candidate records evaluated for HANDBOOK between 632AD and 1000AD. Out of 56.610 candidates, 250 were excluded prior to tabulation to prevent spatial double counting and eliminate unquantified minor scatters, subordinate suburbs merged into metropolitan cores, duplicate aliases and non-settlement architectural fragments. Each retained settlement was assessed on a case-by-case basis by harmonising excavated walled and suburban footprints, period urban densities, *diwan* troop registers and early Islamic geographical treatises (al-Ya'qubi, al-Istakhri, Ibn Hawqal, al-Muqaddasi) with enriched historical and archaeological registers—including the Al-Thurayya Early Islamic Gazetteer, DARMC Mediaeval Major Towns, Euratlas, late-antique continuity anchors from the OXREP Roman Cities Database (Hanson 2016), the Egypt Exploration Society (EES) Delta Survey, the Near East Holocene Urban Settlement Database (Palmisano et al. 2021), From Villages to Empires (Titolo and Palmisano 2025), NERD and C-Turkey—alongside primary morphological and archaeological literature [@Nol2021Defining; @Mokranova2025Material; @Mitchell2021Church], with foundation chronologies and historical toponyms cross-checked against Bosworth's urban reference volume [@Bosworth2007Historic] strictly as a supplemental gazetteer.

Settlement names preserve clean Latin transliteration, while modern national jurisdictions follow current boundaries across 25 states to allow direct comparison with modern geoBoundaries subadministrative units [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Coordinates are reported in decimal degrees (European comma notation) alongside each site's active chronological span inside the 632AD to 1000AD window. Benchmark population columns report 632AD (the Prophet's death), 850AD (the Abbasid zenith) and 1000AD (the turn of the millennium), linearly interpolating between a city's bracketing documented turning points where individual dated observations fall on intermediate years; periods before foundation are marked with a hyphen (-).

# Testing and Validation

Across the 56.360 individually assessed settlements, log-log rank-size regression yields a Zipf exponent $\alpha = 1,22$ ($R^2 = 0,94$), displayed in Figure \ref{fig:settlements-gazetteer}. Mean settlement size shifts from 2.491 inhabitants across 6.301 active centres in 632AD to 726 across 23.633 centres in 750AD, 555 across 42.129 centres at the 850AD Abbasid zenith and 523 across 53.230 centres in 1000AD as lower Iraqi metropolises contracted while Iranian, Egyptian and Maghribi cities and regional itinerary towns expanded. At the top of the distribution sits Baghdad (peaking at 695k in 900AD after its 762AD foundation), followed by Rayy (194k), Samarra (178k in 860AD, founded 836AD), Fustat (174k), Basra (168k), Nishapur (156k), Al-Mada'in (145k), Alexandria (142k), Kufa (132k), Isfahan (132k), Damascus (126k) and Kairouan (124k), producing a strongly structured polycentric rank-size gradient free of artificial tier ceilings.

# Results

## Al-Iraq and Al-Jazira

## Bilad al-Sham and Cyprus

Table \ref{tab:zone2-sham} records 5268 individually assessed settlements across Syria, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Cyprus and Palestine, including Umayyad Damascus, Raqqa, Aleppo (*Halab*), Ramla, Jerusalem, Tyre, Tripoli, Tiberias, Amman and Cypriot Nicosia and Constantia, reflecting dense urban-rural commercial continuity across the Levant [@Bessard2018Politics; @Nol2021Defining; @Mokranova2025Material; @Stern2025Mamluk].

## Iran, Khorasan and Afghanistan

Table \ref{tab:zone4-iran} covers 15918 individually assessed settlements across Iran and Afghanistan, including Rayy, Nishapur, Isfahan, Shiraz, Hamadan, Jurjan, Ahvaz, Ardabil, Siraf, Tus, Qom and Qazvin in Iran alongside Balkh, Herat, Zaranj, Ghazni, Bust and Kabul in Afghanistan, anchoring *qanat*-irrigated oasis agriculture and Silk Road craft manufacture [@Saatsaz2023Technology; @Lu2023Connected; @Michailidis2014Dynastic; @Spooner2019Epilogue].

## Byzantine Anatolia and Caucasia

Table \ref{tab:zone5-anatolia} enumerates 18199 individually assessed centres across Turkey, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia, spanning Byzantine provincial metropolises and *Thughur* border cities (Antioch, Tarsus, Amid, Trebizond, Nicaea, Harran, Mayyafariqin, Malatya, Amorium, Ephesus, Caesarea, Attaleia, Ancyra, Iconium) alongside Transcaucasian capitals and trade hubs (Barda, Ani, Dvin, Tbilisi, Ganja, Shamakhi, Kars and Kutaisi) [@Coleman2021Poleis; @Mitchell2021Church; @Bakirtzis2023Introducin; @Ozbal2026Diet].

## North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula

# Limitations

Three constraints qualify individual settlement entries in this gazetteer. First, metropolitan population trajectories carry genuine archaeological uncertainty - particularly for sprawling multi-quarter capitals such as Abbasid Baghdad (peaking at 695k in 900AD across roughly 7.000 ha of discontinuous urban and garden districts), Samarra (178k in 860AD), Rayy (194k), Fustat (174k) and Nishapur (156k) - where residential housing densities varied widely between dense urban cores and outer *rabad* suburbs [@ALJabri2023Developmen; @Bosworth2007Historic]. Second, the vetted gazetteer restricts tabulation to 56.360 individually documented urban centres, regional capitals and itinerary towns supported by archaeological area measurements, itinerary registers or historical tax assessments (excluding 250 unquantified minor scatters, merged suburbs, duplicate aliases and non-settlement architectural fragments), leaving smaller unquantified rural hamlets to the continuous Matérn kriging surface rather than discrete table rows. Third, where individual cities experienced dated foundation or crisis turning points between canonical regional benchmarks (such as Samarra's 836AD foundation and 860AD peak, Damascus's 745AD Umayyad peak or Amorium's 838AD sack), table columns at 750AD and 850AD linearly interpolate between bracketing documented observations.

# Conclusion

Taken together, the 56.360 individually assessed settlements demonstrate a strongly structured, polycentric urban hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,22$, $R^2 = 0,94$) across the Early Islamic world and Byzantine Anatolia between 632AD and 1000AD. Active urban centres expanded from 6.301 cities housing 15,7M inhabitants in 632AD to 42.129 centres housing 23,4M at the 850AD Abbasid zenith and 53.230 centres housing 27,83M by 1000AD, driven by the seventh-century *amsar* wave, Umayyad foundation towns, Abbasid metropolitan growth at Baghdad and Samarra and resilient oasis urbanisation across Iran, Khurasan, Egypt and the Maghrib.
